messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

We're looking for speakers to present in upcoming Wednesday workshops.

For speakers, we typically have ~20-30 minute talks. That typically are in one of these categories:

 - "How to" - A quick introduction to a topic and pointers to more resources
 - "Show and Tell" - A cool thing you did in R
 - "Here's my problem" - take the group through what you're working on and soliciting feedback

For "How to", I would encourage people to pick topics that they might not know a lot about, but would like to spend a bit of time collecting info and presenting resources (packages, tutorials, etc.)   Upcoming talks will include:

- Interpreting and visualizing mixed models - Stella Copeland
- Data visualization with ggplot - Rosemary Hartman

Here's a list of topics of interest that were solicited through our survey.  If you are interested in talking about any of these, great! But no need to confine yourself to this list:

R Language Basics
-----------------

-   How to do in R the things you do routinely in Excel (ie, data handling).
-   Data Visualization (many requests)
    -   Basics
    -   Improving appearance
    -   Maps + geographical data
-   Best practices in working with data
-   Code organization
    -   Writing tidy functions
-   Using `apply` functions\
-   Dealing with times and dates in R.
-   Digging into package functions

Advanced R language
-------------------

-   Package development
-   Code profiling
-   Manipulating big data in R.
-   Using R interactively with other programs and languages

Statistical topics in R
-----------------------

-   Geostatistics
    -   how to use geomorph package
-   Hierarchical and Bayesian models
    -   Repeated measures statistics
    -   Ordered categorical data
-   Hierarchical and Bayesian models
    -   MCMCglmm
    -   JAGS
-   Overdispersion rules of thumb
-   Network analysis
-   Modeling stochastic processes that are spatially autocorrelated
-   Monte Carlo simulations

Other topics
------------

-   Integral projection models
-   Workflows for sequencing and genomic data

On Wed, Oct 2, 2013 at 1:48 PM, Pedro Martinez-Garcia (UC Davis) <pjmartin...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hello Noam,
>
> I have a question about histogram in ggplot2, do you know if i can obtain a histogram with two scales in y axis? My data have a different magnitude, the first ones are around 800 and the last one are about 10 so we cannot see well the exact number, i dont know how to do it! and if it is possible of course! I am attaching the figure,
>
> Thanks
>
> PJ
>

HI Pedro,

First, please direct questions to the listserv rather than to me - that way you get the benefit of more people's expertise and everyone gets to learn from the Q&A.

The short answer is no.  The author of ggplot specifically disallows this because he thinks it is bad practice.  He elaborates here: http://stackoverflow.com/a/3101876/1757441 . You may want to rescale the data as percentages rather than absolute counts if you want to display them side-by-side.  On the other hand, there are some elaborate ways of hacking this in ggplot, e.g., http://rpubs.com/kohske/dual_axis_in_ggplot2, or you can make the plot in base graphics, adding the second axis with the `axis` function.

Noam

messages.body_plain:
Hi all.

I am trying to reshape some columns of a data frame of repeated measures data collected on a group of people at varying numbers of observation times per person.  The data is structured like this miniature example:

> df <- data.frame(SubID = c(17, 17, 17, 32, 32, 53), Date = as.POSIXct(c("2009-01-23", "2009-01-23", "2009-01-23", "2011-03-13", "2011-03-13", "2010-09-07")), Age = c(27, 27, 27, 39, 39, 60), Gender = c("M", "M", "M", "F", "F", "F"), Obs = c(1372, 2561, 3978, 1576, 2980, 1024), Var1 = c(4.2, 5.1, 2.7, 3.4, 5.6, 3.8), Var2 = c(92.3, 87.5, 102.1, 96.0, 89.3, 99.2))

> df
  SubID       Date Age Gender  Obs Var1  Var2
1    17 2009-01-23  27      M 1372  4.2  92.3
2    17 2009-01-23  27      M 2561  5.1  87.5
3    17 2009-01-23  27      M 3978  2.7 102.1
4    32 2011-03-13  39      F 1576  3.4  96.0
5    32 2011-03-13  39      F 2980  5.6  89.3
6    53 2010-09-07  60      F 1024  3.8  99.2

There is a subject ID for each person, followed by some columns of data about the person (which is always identical within persons), such as the date they filled out the questionnaire, their age, and gender.  Then there is a unique identifier for each observation time followed by the columns of data that were recorded about the person at each time.

I would like to condense the columns of information about each person (which are the same each time) by creating a new data frame of these columns with just one row per person.  So, the desired result would look like this:

   SubID       Date Age Gender
17    17 2009-01-23  27      M
32    32 2011-03-13  39      F
53    53 2010-09-07  60      F

I tried using the reshape function, but it seems to insist on creating a bunch of extra columns for all the time varying variables, which I would then need to remove, since I don't want those for this purpose.  That seems like too much work to ask my computer to do, since the data frame I am actually working with is relatively large.

> reshape(data = df, idvar = "SubID", timevar = "Obs", v.names = c("Var1", "Var2"), direction = "wide")
  SubID       Date Age Gender Var1.1372 Var2.1372 Var1.2561 Var2.2561 Var1.3978
1    17 2009-01-23  27      M       4.2      92.3       5.1      87.5       2.7
4    32 2011-03-13  39      F        NA        NA        NA        NA        NA
6    53 2010-09-07  60      F        NA        NA        NA        NA        NA
  Var2.3978 Var1.1576 Var2.1576 Var1.2980 Var2.2980 Var1.1024 Var2.1024
1     102.1        NA        NA        NA        NA        NA        NA
4        NA       3.4        96       5.6      89.3        NA        NA
6        NA        NA        NA        NA        NA       3.8      99.2

Does anyone know of a way of doing this, either with reshape or a different function, that would allow me to just include the data columns that are the same for each repetition of each person?  Thank you very much for any help or ideas!

Bonnie

messages.body_plain:
This is the canonical example of what the plyr::ddply() is for:
library(plyr)
ddply(df, .(SubID), summarize, SubID=SubID[1], Date=Date[1], Age=Age[1], Gender=Gender[1])

This breaks up df into chunks by SubID, summarizes each chunk by making a data frame where each of the columns are the first value of the chunk's columns, then re-assembles into a new data frame.

If your data table is very large, it may be worth using data.table to do this:
library(data.table)
dt = data.table(df)
dt[, lapply(.SD, function(x) x[1]), by=SubID, .SDcols=c("SubID", "Date", "Age", "Gender") ]

or
dt[, list(SubID=SubID[1], Date=Date[1], Age=Age[1], Gender=Gender[1]), by=SubID]

This is slightly less intuitive. To create a multiple-column output in data.table, you need to create a list of your output columns. The first version does this with lapply, and the variable .SDcols is a proxy for a list of the selected columns. The second just creates the list explicitly.

 - Noam

messages.body_plain:
Fellow R users;

Is anyone familiar with circular statistics?

I have some data on the time of day when people went to bed over several nights of sleep (in decimal hours on a 24 hour clock).  Here is an example:

> sleep <- data.frame(person.id <http://person.id> = c(117, 117, 117, 208, 265, 265, 327, 327, 327, 327), bedtime = c(23.2, NA, 21.5, NA, 0.7, 1.3, 23.6, 0.5, 22.9, 1.1))
> sleep
   person.id <http://person.id> bedtime
1        117    23.2
2        117      NA
3        117    21.5
4        208      NA
5        265     0.7
6        265     1.3
7        327    23.6
8        327     0.5
9        327    22.9
10       327     1.1

I would like to calculate each person's average bedtime.  Doing this the same way that I would normally calculate an average does not produce meaningful results because time of day is a circular scale (similar to angles or compass bearings), and sometimes people go to bed before midnight, other times, after.

> tapply(sleep$bedtime, sleep$person.id <http://person.id>, mean, na.rm = TRUE)
   117    208    265    327
22.350    NaN  1.000 12.025

Does anyone know how to calculate an average time of day?  (I found this webpage <http://rosettacode.org/wiki/Averages/Mean_time_of_day>, which addresses the topic, but does not provide an example of how to do it in R. I also got the package, circular, which provides functions for circular statistics, but I'm struggling with figuring out how to use it for this operation.)  Thanks for any ideas.

Bonnie

Just realized a typo. names should be names <- names(models), otherwise if you change the name of the dlply() output it won't work.

combo.out <- function(models, labels=FALSE){
names = names(models)

n = unlist(lapply(models, function(x) x$n))
SMAintercept = unlist(lapply(models, function(x) x$regression.results[x$regression.results$Method =="SMA",][2]))
SMAslope = unlist(lapply(models, function(x) x$regression.results[x$regression.results$Method =="SMA",][3]))
r = unlist(lapply(models, function(x) x$r))
rsquare = unlist(lapply(models, function(x) x$rsquare))
p = unlist(lapply(models, function(x) x$P.param))

df <- data.frame(names, n, SMAintercept, SMAslope, r, rsquare,p)
row.names(df) <- NULL
return(df)
}

messages.body_plain:
Hi folks, I have a set of data from which I need to estimate parameters for an equation that explains a shift towards resistance in the fungal disease of pines that I work with. The equation is:

y = (M*x) / (a + x)

where "y" is the proportional reduction in lesion size and "x" is the number of previous infections. I need to calculate "M" (maximum possible reduction in lesion length) and "a" (number of infections needed to reach half of M). I'm assuming there is something that should work for me in the generalized nonlinear models (gnm) package, but I don't really know where to start. Any thoughts? Thanks

Greg
